title: The Idea of Atoms
objective: After this level you can explain how the idea of atoms began with the ancient Greeks.
summary: In the 5th century BCE, Leucippus and Democritus reasoned that cutting matter must stop at uncuttable atoms moving through the void. Aristotle disagreed; proof waited until the 1800s.

cards.headline: Cut a crumb in half. Then again. How long can you keep going?
cards.body: Forever, said some ancient thinkers. Two Greeks said no: sooner or later you hit a piece too small to cut. They had no microscope and no lab, only an argument. It gave us the word atom.

cards.fact: In the 5th century BCE, Leucippus and his student Democritus said all matter is made of tiny particles called atoms.
cards.context: The name comes from the Greek for "indivisible" or "uncuttable": an atom was meant to be the last piece, the one no knife could split. Remember Level 3, where all matter turned out to be made of tiny particles? This is where that idea began, about 2,400 years ago.

cards.headline: An argument, not an experiment
cards.body: Their reasoning went like this. Suppose you could cut anything in half forever, and then imagine finishing the job. What is left? If it is specks of dust, you haven't finished cutting. If it is nothing at all, how could a pile of nothings add up to a crumb? So the cutting must stop somewhere: at the atom. Notice what is missing. These philosophers never tested their idea with an experiment; they argued it.

cards.headline: Atoms and the void
cards.body: Democritus pictured atoms moving through empty space, the void, and differing only in shape, size, arrangement and position. Ancient writers compared them to letters: A differs from N in shape, and AN differs from NA in arrangement. A few letters spell every word. Even sweetness, Democritus said, exists only "by convention"; in reality there are just atoms and void.

mascot.line: So a crumb is just a very long word. Delicious spelling.

cards.headline: The idea that waited
cards.body: Not everyone agreed. Aristotle rejected atoms: he held that matter could be divided forever and was made of fire, earth, air and water. A scientific atomic theory, one that explained how matter actually behaves, arrived only in the early 1800s. The Greeks had the right hunch. It just took a very long time to prove.

cards.headline: Atoms: imagined
learned: Leucippus and Democritus imagined atoms in the 5th century BCE
Atom means "indivisible": the piece you can't cut
They reasoned it out and never tested it
Atoms move through the void and differ in shape and arrangement

questions.prompt: What did the Greek word behind "atom" originally mean?

options.label: Invisible
options.rationale: Atoms are invisible, but that isn't what the name means.

options.label: Heavy
options.rationale: The name says nothing about weight.

options.label: Everywhere
options.rationale: The name is about cutting, not location.

questions.explanation: Atom comes from the Greek for "indivisible": the piece that can't be cut any further.

questions.prompt: Why did Leucippus and Democritus think cutting a crumb in half, again and again, must stop somewhere?

options.label: They cut crumbs and saw the atoms
options.rationale: They had no microscope and ran no experiments.

options.label: Their knives were too blunt to go on
options.rationale: The argument was about logic, not tools.

options.label: Cutting forever leads to a contradiction

questions.explanation: Finishing an endless division leaves either specks you could still cut, or nothings that can't add up to a crumb. So the cutting must stop at atoms.

questions.prompt: Level 3 said a gas's particles are far apart. In Democritus's picture, what fills the gaps between atoms?

options.label: Air, the fourth element
options.rationale: That is Aristotle's four-element picture, which rejected atoms.

options.label: Smaller atoms packed in tight
options.rationale: Democritus's atoms were the smallest pieces.

options.label: Water that holds them together
options.rationale: The atomists put nothing between atoms.

questions.explanation: Democritus pictured atoms moving through the void, empty space, which fits the modern picture of gas particles far apart.
